title: This Can't Be Normal
author: Barbara Schindler
summary: Executive coach Barbara Schindler introduces her podcast conversation with Chanie Wilschanski, founder of Schools of Excellence and author of This Can't Be Normal, in a written post that lays out the episode's core arguments. The central idea is the 'invisible weight of leadership': the constant noticing, anticipating, and tracking that keeps leaders awake even when their systems and teams are technically functioning. Schindler highlights Wilschanski's claim that competence, the trait that built a leader's success, can become a trap that keeps them the answer person for everyone. The post points to a coaching example in which a worry about ordering crayons escalates in ten questions to a fear of jail, illustrating why simply telling overwhelmed leaders to delegate rarely works. It also draws on Wilschanski's marriage practice of a standing, pre-decided Tuesday breakfast as a model for rhythms that hold regardless of mood. The written notes include takeaways and action steps, making the post substantive beyond a bare episode listing.
points: The 'invisible weight of leadership' names the mental load of noticing and anticipating that persists even when a leader's organization is running well on paper.
Wilschanski argues that competence, left unchecked, becomes a dependency trap in which the leader remains everyone's default answer.
Walking a nagging worry 'downstream' out loud, as in the crayons example, exposes catastrophizing and explains why generic advice to delegate fails.
Shielding a team from consequences prevents change, because people rarely move until the cost of staying put exceeds the cost of the alternative.
Effective rhythms, like a standing weekly breakfast or a fixed stopping time, work because they are decided in calm and do not bend to mood.
quotes: Chanie works with school owners and organizational leaders who have built real, thriving businesses and still feel like they’re drowning. Not because anything is broken on paper.

Because of what she calls the invisible weight of leadership, the noticing, anticipating, and tracking that keeps running at 3am even when your systems, your team, and your checklists are all technically doing their job.
We get into why competence, the very trait that built your success, can quietly become the thing keeping you dependent on being needed.
It’s one of the clearest explanations I’ve heard for why telling an overwhelmed leader to just delegate almost never works.

We also talk about the rhythm she and her husband have built into their marriage, a standing Tuesday breakfast that’s pre-decided in calm and doesn’t bend to how either of them is feeling that week, and how that same structure applies to knowing when to close your laptop for the day.
People rarely change until the cost of staying still outweighs the cost of the alternative. Protecting your team from consequences keeps them from ever getting there.
Take the one thing keeping you up at night and walk it downstream, out loud, the way Chanie does with her client and the crayons, until you can see what would actually happen.
